title: Add explicit request timeouts to the yfinance/Stooq market-data provider calls
description:
Found while diagnosing why the ticker detail view (GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis) was very slow (conversation session, 2026-09-29): the cause wasn't IBKR (confirmed -- swing mode never touches ibkr_provider, and GET /api/ibkr/status stayed fast throughout). Yahoo Finance was rate-limiting this environment (confirmed directly: a fresh request to https://query1.finance.yahoo.com/... returned HTTP 429) after a burst of real requests. Neither YFinanceProvider nor StooqProvider sets an explicit timeout on its outbound HTTP calls (yfinance's own internal default is 30s per underlying call, unset/unoverridden by this app's provider code) -- and get_analysis/_compute_signal fetch daily OHLCV, weekly OHLCV, and extended data sequentially (three separate blocking calls per ticker), so a degraded provider can stack close to 90+ seconds of latency for one ticker. Because each of those runs on FastAPI's shared worker-thread pool and nothing cancels a request a client has already given up on, this compounded under this session's testing load into genuine resource exhaustion: the live dev backend process was directly observed holding 125 live threads, at which point even trivial, unrelated endpoints (GET /docs, a static page; GET /api/ibkr/status, no provider call at all) became unresponsive too -- confirmed by requesting them concurrently with a stuck request. For comparison, the identical fetch-analyse-zones pipeline run directly in a fresh Python process with a warm cache completed in well under 1 second, showing the cost is in the request-handling layer under load, not the computation itself.

This is a real, generally-applicable robustness gap (not specific to today's rate-limiting spike) -- any future Yahoo Finance outage, rate-limit, or network degradation will reproduce the same cascading slowdown for every user of this app, not just fail the one affected ticker.

checklist.step: Add an explicit, reasoned timeout to every outbound yfinance HTTP call in YFinanceProvider (yfinance's Ticker.history()/other calls accept a timeout= kwarg passed through to the underlying request -- confirmed present in the installed yfinance package's own data.py, default 30s per call today if unset). Decide and record (decisions entry) the chosen value, trading off failing fast under a real outage against not killing a legitimately-slow-but-working fetch.
Check whether StooqProvider's own HTTP fetch (_fetch_csv) has an explicit timeout today; add one with the same reasoning if not.

Research and decide (decisions entry) whether GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's sequential daily -> weekly -> extended-data fetch (app/api/routers/stocks.py's get_analysis) should become concurrent, mirroring the ThreadPoolExecutor pattern this codebase already uses elsewhere for the same reason (app.api.day_trader_signal.compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently, app.portfolio.pricing's per-position concurrent fetch) -- so a slow provider adds its cost once per ticker rather than up to three times.

Verify a provider timeout surfaces through the existing DataProviderUnavailableError -> 503 path (docs/architecture/API.md), not as an unhandled exception -- this app's already-documented graceful-degradation contract for the data layer.

Tests: a mocked slow/hanging provider call that exceeds the new timeout, asserting it fails fast with the expected DataProviderUnavailableError rather than hanging -- no live network calls, per docs/architecture/Testing.md.

decisions.decision: Chose a 10-second per-request timeout for every outbound yfinance HTTP call (both `Ticker.history()`'s own `timeout=` kwarg in `YFinanceProvider._fetch`, and a session-level clamp -- see the next decision -- for `get_extended_data`'s `.calendar`/`.info`/`.insider_transactions`), matching `StooqProvider`'s pre-existing `timeout=10` (stooq_provider.py's `_fetch_csv`).
decisions.rationale: 10s gives both providers the same per-request budget, so a degraded source fails at a predictable, consistent latency regardless of which one is being called. Rejected 30s (yfinance's own current unset-default for `.info`/`.calendar`/`.insider_transactions`, per `yfinance/data.py`'s `get`/`get_raw_json`): that's exactly the value that, times the three sequential get_extended_data property fetches plus the daily/weekly `.history()` calls, produced this task's own ~90s+ incident -- keeping it would leave the root cause unfixed. Rejected a much tighter value (e.g. 3-5s): Yahoo's chart/quote endpoints can legitimately take a few seconds under ordinary (non-degraded) load, especially for the `.info`/`calendar` quote-summary endpoints, which are heavier queries than the plain OHLCV chart endpoint; a too-tight cap would turn normal peak-hour latency into spurious 503s, trading one reliability problem for another. 10s is generous enough to absorb that while still bounding the worst case to a small, fixed multiple of itself instead of an effectively unbounded stack.

decisions.decision: Implemented the yfinance timeout via two mechanisms: (1) pass `timeout=` directly on the `.history()` call (`_fetch`), and (2) a `_clamp_session_timeout` helper that wraps the underlying `YfData` singleton session's `.request()` method in place, reached via `Ticker._data._session` (private attributes), to cap `.calendar`/`.info`/`.insider_transactions` as well -- rather than building an app-owned `requests.Session()` and passing it to `yf.Ticker(ticker, session=...)`.
decisions.rationale: Investigated the installed yfinance package (1.7.0) directly: `.history()` accepts a `timeout=` kwarg (default already 10s in this version, contrary to the task description's blanket '30s per call' framing, which turned out to describe `yfinance/data.py`'s lower-level `get`/`get_raw_json`/`post` default rather than every call site) and passes it through to the actual HTTP request. But `Ticker.calendar`/`.info`/`.insider_transactions` (used by `get_extended_data`) are plain properties with no `timeout=` parameter at all in this version -- confirmed by reading `yfinance/scrapers/quote.py`/`ticker.py` -- so there is no public per-call override for them; they fall through to `data.py`'s 30s default today, and three of those calls stacking is the single biggest contributor to the ~90s incident this task exists to fix. A session-level clamp is the only way to bound them. Rejected building a fresh app-owned session and injecting it via `yf.Ticker(ticker, session=my_session)`: yfinance's `YfData` (the object that actually issues every request) is a process-wide singleton, so the *first* `yf.Ticker(...)` call in the process determines its permanent session -- if that first call ever passed a bare `requests.Session()`, it would replace yfinance's own curl_cffi-backed TLS/browser-fingerprinting session (`yfinance._http.new_session`, preferred specifically because it reduces Yahoo rate-limiting/blocking risk) for the rest of the process, making the exact 429/blocking problem this task is fixing *worse*. Reaching into the session yfinance already built for itself and wrapping `.request()` in place preserves that fingerprinting while still bounding every request. Accepted the cost of touching private attributes (`Ticker._data`, `YfData._session`) for this: `_clamp_session_timeout` and `_new_ticker` are both defensive (`getattr`/`AttributeError`-guarded, silently no-op rather than raise) so a future yfinance internals change degrades this specific extended-data protection rather than breaking every fetch -- `.history()`'s own inline `timeout=` is unaffected either way.

decisions.decision: Confirmed `StooqProvider._fetch_csv`'s existing `urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10)` (stooq_provider.py:110) is adequate as-is; no code change made to StooqProvider.
decisions.rationale: 10s matches the yfinance-side timeout chosen above, giving both data sources the same per-request budget. `urllib.request.urlopen`'s timeout already raises `socket.timeout`/`URLError` on expiry, which `_fetch_daily`'s existing broad `except Exception` already converts to `DataProviderUnavailableError` -- no additional error-handling change needed on the Stooq side.

decisions.decision: Converted GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's daily/weekly/extended-data fetch from sequential to concurrent, via `ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)` in `get_analysis` (app/api/routers/stocks.py), resolving `.result()` in the same daily -> weekly -> extended order as the previous sequential calls.
decisions.rationale: None of the three fetches depends on either of the others, so running them concurrently means a slow/degraded provider now costs its ~10s timeout budget once per ticker instead of up to three times -- directly addressing the compounding-latency mechanism (three sequential ~30s-capable calls stacking toward ~90s) that produced this task's own incident. Mirrors the already-established, already-reviewed `ThreadPoolExecutor` pattern this same file's `get_indicator_history` uses for its own daily+weekly concurrent fetch (backend-indicator-history-performance), and the pattern `app.api.day_trader_signal.compute_day_trader_signals_concurrently`/`app.portfolio.pricing` use for N-ticker fan-out. Resolving `.result()` in daily-then-weekly-then-extended order (rather than, say, whichever completes first) preserves the exact pre-existing error-priority behavior (a daily failure -> 404/422/503 takes priority over a weekly/extended one) so no existing error-mapping test needed to change. Verified safe against `CachedDataProvider`'s SQLite-backed cache layer without any cache-layer change: `get_extended_data` already takes the same `self._lock` `get_daily_ohlcv`/`get_weekly_ohlcv` do (app/data/cache.py), which was already documented and reviewed as safe for exactly this kind of concurrent-caller addition when the daily+weekly pair was made concurrent for backend-indicator-history-performance.

decisions.decision: Fixed PR #360's needs_work finding by replacing GET /api/stocks/{ticker}/analysis's `with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3) as executor:` block with manual executor lifecycle management: `executor = ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=3)` followed by a `try`/`finally` where the `finally` calls `executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)` instead of relying on the context manager's implicit `shutdown(wait=True)`. `.result()` is still resolved in daily -> weekly -> extended order, preserving the exact same error-priority behavior (a daily failure takes priority over weekly/extended) that both the original sequential code and the first version of this concurrency fix already established.
decisions.rationale: `ThreadPoolExecutor.__exit__` unconditionally calls `shutdown(wait=True)`, which blocks until every submitted future completes before an exception raised by an earlier `.result()` call can propagate out of the `with` block -- pr-reviewer reproduced this directly on PR #360 (a stub whose daily fetch raised immediately still took ~3.04s to return its 404 because `get_extended_data` was sleeping 3s). `shutdown(wait=False)` returns immediately without waiting for in-flight futures, so `.result()`'s exception now propagates the moment it's raised, regardless of how long the other two legs take. `cancel_futures=True` (Python 3.9+) is included for correctness/future-proofing even though with `max_workers=3` == the number of futures submitted here, all three tasks start immediately on submission and none are left queued for it to actually cancel -- if a future edit ever oversubscribes this executor (more futures than workers), `cancel_futures` would then cancel the ones still queued. Rejected switching to `concurrent.futures.as_completed` with early-cancel-on-first-failure: because all three futures start immediately (queue-less with `max_workers` == submitted count), `as_completed` wouldn't stop the other two from running anyway (cancel() returns False once a future is already executing), so it would add complexity (reordering results by which ticket resolved first, then re-deriving the intended daily->weekly->extended priority for the actually-failed one) without fixing anything `shutdown(wait=False)` doesn't already fix more simply. Rejected fully serializing the fetch to eliminate the 'all three calls issued unconditionally even when the first would short-circuit' side effect entirely: that would give up the actual overlap benefit this task exists to provide for the common (all-succeed) case, and the reviewer's finding centered on the fail-fast latency delay, not on eliminating that overhead in the failure case -- the already-filed backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups task's own checklist doesn't ask for that either. Worker threads for the two still-running legs are not leaked: they are pool-owned, keep running to natural completion after `shutdown(wait=False)` (which only stops the pool from accepting new work and doesn't block the caller), and their results (if any) are simply never collected since nothing calls `.result()`/`.exception()` on their futures again -- confirmed no unhandled-future-exception warning is emitted either way. Verified with a genuinely discriminating regression test (`TestConcurrentFetch.test_fast_daily_failure_returns_promptly_despite_slow_other_legs`, tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis.py): mutation-tested by temporarily reverting to the blocking `with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor:` form, confirming the new test fails (elapsed climbs to ~1.0s instead of staying under 0.5s), then restoring the fix and confirming it passes again.

comments.summary: Blocking (new, different bug from the first review round -- the fail-fast-delay bug that round found is genuinely fixed): get_analysis's new `executor.shutdown(wait=False, cancel_futures=True)` lets an already-running weekly/extended leg keep executing in the background after the response is returned. Those legs write through CachedDataProvider (app/data/cache.py), which shares the exact same SQLAlchemy Session the request's own `db: Session = Depends(get_db)` resolves to (dependency caching -- same Session instance). get_db's `finally: db.close()` (app/db/session.py:27) runs on the request-handling thread as soon as get_analysis returns/raises, which can now happen before an abandoned leg finishes its own self._db.commit()/query() inside _upsert/_upsert_extended -- the exact 'two threads touching one Session at once' bug class CachedDataProvider's own docstring already documents from PR #231, just reintroduced via a different path (early return + abandoned background thread, rather than two concurrently-awaited futures). Reproduced directly (not just by inspection): real CachedDataProvider (not the get_data_provider test override, which bypasses this entirely) with a stub where get_daily_ohlcv raises immediately, get_weekly_ohlcv returns almost instantly, and get_extended_data sleeps 1s before its cache write -- hitting the real FastAPI app with the real get_db/SessionLocal machinery produced `sqlalchemy.exc.IllegalStateChangeError: Method 'close()' can't be called here; method '_prepare_impl()' is already in progress` on roughly 30-40% of runs (multiple runs across two separate batches), raised from get_db's db.close() while the abandoned extended-data leg's _upsert_extended was mid-commit on the same Session in a different thread. Worse than a merely-swallowed background exception: this happens inside FastAPI's dependency-teardown AsyncExitStack.__aexit__, which runs before the response is sent -- every failing run never returned a response to the client at all (TestClient.get() raised instead of returning), meaning in production the request this fix was supposed to make return a clean fast 404 can instead fail outright some fraction of the time under exactly the 'abandoned other leg still running when the fast leg fails' scenario this PR targets. Separately (not reproduced, follows directly from concurrent.futures semantics): an abandoned leg's own fetch exception that isn't from this session race (e.g. a genuine DataProviderUnavailableError) is never surfaced via .result()/.exception(), so it's silently discarded with no log line -- the decisions entry's 'no unhandled-future-exception warning is emitted' is accurate but not reassuring, since that's exactly the problem (a real failure becomes invisible). cancel_futures=True doesn't help here since with max_workers=3 == futures submitted, every leg starts immediately and none are left queued to cancel.

review.notes: Confirmed the first review round's fail-fast-delay bug is genuinely fixed: reran my original repro (daily fails immediately, another leg sleeps 3s) against the current branch -- 404 now returns in ~0.05s. Reran the mutation test myself: reverted get_analysis to the blocking `with ThreadPoolExecutor(...) as executor:` form -> test_fast_daily_failure_returns_promptly_despite_slow_other_legs fails (1.03s vs 0.5s threshold) -> `git checkout --` to restore -> passes again, tree clean. Confirmed error-priority behavior unchanged for the normal case (all 33 tests in tests/integration/test_stocks_analysis.py pass, including the pre-existing daily>weekly>extended priority tests). Independently re-ran: full backend suite (1482 passed, 99.92% coverage, gate 90%), ruff/mypy clean, scripts/validate_tasks.py clean (347 files), backend/openapi.json regenerated with zero diff (correct no-op -- this PR touches no route/schema). No frontend changes in this PR (gh pr diff --name-only: backend + docs/tasks only), so steps 9/9a's browser walkthrough and e2e suite don't apply -- noted explicitly rather than skipped silently. Verified backend-data-provider-timeouts-followups's 4 non-blocking findings from the first round are all still present, unduplicated, state still planned -- no changes needed there this round since this round's finding is blocking, not a follow-up candidate (a real, frequently-reproducible correctness regression on the exact code path this task is hardening, not a pre-existing gap being surfaced, so it needs a real fix before merge rather than being tracked and shipped). Did not prescribe a specific fix (task-worker's call to make and record as a decisions entry), but flagged some directions in the PR comment: not returning until every self._db-touching leg has finished; giving abandoned legs' cache writes their own DB session independent of the request's; or awaiting (with a bound) any future that started touching self._db before letting the request's own session close. Posted as a COMMENTED-type PR review (gh pr review --comment), not approve/request-changes. State set back to implementing so task-worker can fix this and a fresh review can follow. (Also corrected an inconsistency found on this task's own state field: it read 'testing' going into this review despite the prior review's own notes saying it had been set back to 'implementing' -- setting it to 'implementing' now per this verdict resolves that regardless of how it drifted.)
